newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bosnian leaders accept peace stabilisation plan.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian leaders accept peace stabilisation plan.

text.p: Bosnia's three co-presidents agreed with world powers on Thursday on a detailed plan to stabilise the fragile peace in the former Yugoslav republic over the next two years as a condition for continuing international aid.

But Western powers differed publicly at a Paris conference over the duration of an extended mandate for a NATO-led peace force, and the United States warned Bosnia's factions they could face U.N. sanctions if they fail to restore freedom of movement in the ethnically divided country.

The accord approved at the three-hour meeting provides a transitional period to make the peace negotiated a year ago in Dayton, Ohio, self-sustaining and build joint institutions, a functioning economy and a more normal life for Bosnians.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, who co-chaired the conference, said it had adopted "a contract between the leaders of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the international community" in which aid was conditional on compliance.
"We will respect this contract strictly...but it is first and foremost the leaders of Bosnia-Herzegovina who must fully accept their responsiblity," he told a news conference.

The co-presidents -- Moslem Alija Izetbegovic, Serb Momcilo Krajisnik and Croat Kresimir Zubak -- pledged to complete Bosnia's joint institutions "as soon as possible" and accepted a 13-point plan to fulfil implementation of the Dayton accord.
It commits them to allow freedom of movement, facilitate the return of refugees, cooperate with the international war crimes tribunal and increase democracy and press freedom.
Izetbegovic told reporters he wanted a joint cabinet formed in time for a follow-up conference in London early next month.

The document did not commit the international community to keep a military presence when the current Peace Implementation Force (IFOR) mandate expires next month, although it recognised "the fundamental importance of a secure environment to the task of civilian implementation".
In Washington, NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said the United States was preparing to take part with as many as 8,000 troops in a new force of up to 30,000 next year.

International mediator Carl Bildt, whose powers were increased at the conference, said the peace process was "not yet self-sustaining" and a successor force must stay for the entire two-year consolidation period. De Charette also said the force should be wound down over two years.

However, German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said Bonn wanted it limited to one year. It would be wrong to give the rival Bosnian factions the impression that international aid could be dragged out over several years, he said.
"Our position is crystal clear. One year," Kinkel said.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher told the meeting: "We have made it clear to the parties that the Security Council will consider imposing measures if they fail to significantly meet their obligations under the peace agreement."

He said the Bosnians would be under close scrutiny regarding freedom of movement and the return of refugees. Aid would also depend on their handing over suspects to the war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

Senior U.S. official John Kornblum held late-night talks to press the three leaders into agreeing a joint cabinet structure, but Bosnian officials said little progress was made. Bosnian state radio said Izetbegovic had resented sharp U.S. pressure.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind summed up the message to Bosnia's leaders when he told reporters: "The international effort should not be taken for granted. They must not assume that we will be there whatever they do.
"It must be dependent on the Bosnian parties showing their willingness to take forward the process of nation building. There's been some progress but not enough," he said.

At a closing ceremony, French President Jacques Chirac, flanked by the Bosnian co-presidents on their first joint appearance on the international scene, said the conference had opened "a new, concrete and important stage in peace taking root in Bosnia".
